practice_span: I have been making these since I was ten. Now it has been twenty-two years.
local_belonging_phrase: “Sikki grows on the edge of our pond. If there's no mauni at a daughter's farewell, what kind of farewell is it?”
ecological_input: After the rains, sikki grass grows along ponds and rivers. Drying it in the sun brings out its golden colour.
place_change: Ponds were filled in and fields grew. Now we must go far for sikki, and nobody can tell when the flood will come.
emotion_about_place_change: “As the grass gets less, it feels like an old relation is moving away.”
teaching_memory: My mother had me make the lid of my first mauni. It came out crooked. She showed it to my grandmother and said, “Look, my daughter made this.” She did not correct it.
family_generations: My grandmother, my mother and me. My daughter Gudiya is fourteen, and sits and learns in the evenings.
material_origin: From nearby ponds and riverbanks. Colours from the Madhubani market.
material_in_hands: Wet sikki bends under the takua and doesn't break. If too dry, it snaps with a sound.
occasion_of_use: A daughter's farewell, weddings, and mauni and baskets at the time of Chhath.
strength_anchor: I can make very fine small maunis, and the right count of flowers and leaves settles by hand.
